findings.title: Google refresh persists the Zod result and corrupts the credential
findings.body: After a Google token refresh, the value written to Credential.key is the object returned by parseRefreshTokenResponse, which is the Zod safeParse wrapper ({success, data}) rather than the credential object. Previously googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the tokens themselves. The next GoogleCalendarService construction calls googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) and throws because access_token is nested under data, so every Google calendar stops working after the first refresh (typically within an hour). This runs even when credential sync is disabled. When sync is enabled it is also wrong in a second way: refreshOAuthTokens returns an unparsed fetch Response, so res.data is undefined and token.access_token throws before a usable token is applied.

findings.title: Salesforce client always refreshes, then crashes on missing prisma
findings.body: getClient now refreshes the Salesforce token on every CalendarService construction, then calls prisma.credential.update, but prisma is never imported in this file. That throws ReferenceError, the Connection is never returned, and every Salesforce calendar/CRM operation fails after deploy. Even if the import is added, the jsforce Connection is still built with credentialKey.access_token (the pre-refresh token) rather than the access token just fetched, and a failed refresh now takes down calls that previously relied on a still-valid access token. Enabling credential sync makes this worse: parseRefreshTokenResponse switches to the minimum schema, strips instance_url and the other Salesforce fields, and the update overwrites the stored key with that stripped object.

findings.title: Parser invents refresh_token and drops every other token field
findings.body: If the parsed payload has no refresh_token, this sets refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token" and returns that object. Office 365 marks refresh_token optional and then spreads the parsed data over the stored credential (office365calendar CalendarService), so a normal Microsoft refresh that omits a new refresh token permanently replaces the real refresh token and the next refresh cannot succeed. The minimum schema used when sync is enabled does not do what the comments say: [z.string().toString()] is a literal key, not a catchall, and z.object strips unknown keys, so expiry_date, expires_in, instance_url, and similar fields are discarded. Callers that persist the result (Zoom, Salesforce, Office 365) then save an incomplete key and, via this stub, a fake refresh token.

findings.title: Sync refresh returns a raw Response that callers cannot use
findings.body: When CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set, this returns the fetch Response and never checks response.ok or parses JSON. Callers were not updated to that contract. HubSpot and both Zoho services expect an axios/SDK body with .data or accessToken/expiresIn and will throw or write a non-token value into Credential.key. Google reads res.data. Lark, Webex, and Zoom expect provider-specific JSON (Lark's code/data envelope, Webex's strict scope schema, Zoom's expires_in) and will fail or, in Zoom's case, persist NaN expiry and the stub refresh token. The request also sends only calcomUserId and appSlug, with no documented response schema that those adapters share, so turning the feature on breaks token refresh for the wired apps instead of refreshing them.

findings.title: Outbound token sync sends no shared secret
findings.body: The sync POST that is supposed to return a third-party access token authenticates nothing: no CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, Authorization header, or signed timestamp, only calcomUserId and appSlug. The inbound webhook requires the shared secret, but the call that actually dispenses live OAuth access tokens does not. A self-hoster implementing the contract this client calls (the comment says the response should contain the access token and expiry) exposes user access tokens to anyone who can reach that URL and guess or enumerate a user id.

findings.title: Credential sync updates an arbitrary row and can duplicate keys
findings.body: The handler finds a credential with findFirst({userId, appId}) and no orderBy, then updates only that id. (userId, appId) is not unique: Google's OAuth callback always inserts a new credential row, and two concurrent webhook calls can both observe no row and both create. findFirst may therefore update a credential that is not the one calendar/video code loads, so the webhook returns success while the live tokens stay stale, or it creates duplicates that later refreshes keep splitting. The update path also never sets invalid: false, so a credential already marked invalid stays unusable after the source of truth pushes new keys. Zod parse and symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse are uncaught, so a bad body or ciphertext becomes an unhandled 500 instead of a 4xx.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sync sends credential id as the user id
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens's third argument is the Cal.com user id, but refreshAccessToken passes credentialId. When credential sync is enabled, the parent app looks up tokens for whatever user has that numeric id, not the owner of this credential. If parsing is later fixed to accept the sync response, those tokens are written onto this credential, so one user can be given another user's Zoho access token. With the current fetch Response return value, tokenInfo.data is undefined and refresh throws instead.

findings.title: Zoom sync uses app slug zoomvideo instead of zoom
findings.body: The refresh call passes appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom credential is stored with appId "zoom" (see the OAuth callback) and the installed-app path uses slug "zoom". The webhook and the parent app store key off the real slug, so a sync refresh asks for an app that does not exist and will not return this user's Zoom tokens. Other adapters in this PR pass the real slug (google-calendar, msteams, office365-calendar).

findings.title: No tests for credential write or token-refresh regressions
findings.body: The new webhook can create or overwrite OAuth credential JSON for any user, and the shared refresh helpers change the success path for Google, Office 365, Zoom, and Salesforce even when sync is off. The PR adds no tests, and the checklist confirms none were run. A test that refreshes a Google or Office 365 credential with sync disabled, and one that posts a valid webhook payload, would have caught the safeParse object being stored and the literal refresh_token overwrite before merge.
